Pros:
• Easy to understand and visualize
• Handles categorical & numerical data
• Captures non-linear relationships
• Requires little preprocessing (no scaling)
• Handles missing values and outliers fairly well
• Fast training & prediction
• Provides feature importance
Cons:
• Prone to overfitting (especially deep trees)
• Unstable — small data changes can alter structure
• Greedy splits may miss global optimum
• Poor extrapolation beyond training data
• Produces step-like regression outputs
Use Cases:
• Credit risk scoring
• Medical decision support
• Customer churn analysis
• Education analytics
• Explainable business rules

Pros:
• Reduces overfitting via ensemble averaging
• Robust to noise & outliers
• Handles non-linear data well
• Works with large feature sets
• Provides reliable feature importance
• Supports both regression & classification
Cons:
• Less interpretable than a single tree
• Slower training/inference for large data
• Memory-intensive (stores many trees)
• Slight bias toward features with many levels
• Not ideal for sparse, text-like data
Use Cases:
• Fraud detection
• Healthcare analytics
• E-commerce recommendations
• Manufacturing defect prediction
• Financial forecasting

Pros:
• Excellent for high-dimensional data (text, images)
• Works well with clear class separation
• Kernel trick models complex non-linear patterns
• Robust generalization on small/medium data
• Memory-efficient — depends on support vectors
Cons:
• Computationally expensive for large datasets
• Requires kernel & parameter tuning
• Sensitive to noise and overlapping classes
• No direct probability outputs
• Not easily interpretable
Use Cases:
• Image & handwriting recognition
• Text categorization / spam filtering
• Sentiment analysis
• Facial recognition
• Disease classification

Pros:
• Very simple and intuitive
• No training phase (lazy learner)
• Works well with well-distributed data
• Naturally handles multi-class problems
• Non-parametric — no assumption about data distribution
Cons:
• Slow prediction on large datasets (computes distance for all points)
• Requires scaling of features
• Sensitive to irrelevant features & noise
• Struggles in high dimensions (curse of dimensionality)
• Storage-intensive
Use Cases:
• Recommendation systems
• Image recognition (e.g., handwritten digits)
• Pattern recognition
• Medical similarity analysis
• Anomaly detection

Pros:
• Simple, fast, and interpretable
• Provides probability estimates
• Performs well for linearly separable data
• Robust to small noise
• Regularization available to prevent overfitting (L1/L2)
• Works well with large, sparse datasets
Cons:
• Only models linear decision boundaries (unless features engineered)
• Sensitive to outliers
• Requires feature scaling
• May underperform on non-linear relationships
• Assumes independent features
Use Cases:
• Binary & multi-class classification (One-vs-Rest)
• Marketing lead scoring
• Credit approval / fraud detection
• Medical diagnosis (e.g., disease risk)
• Text sentiment analysis

Pros:
• Extremely fast and efficient
• Works well on high-dimensional text data
• Requires very little training data
• Handles multi-class problems naturally
• Simple and interpretable
• Robust to irrelevant features
Cons:
• Assumes feature independence (often unrealistic)
• Struggles with correlated features
• Zero-frequency problem for unseen values
• Continuous variables require distribution assumptions
• May underperform with small sample sizes
Use Cases:
• Spam filtering
• Text / document classification
• Sentiment analysis
• Medical text categorization
• Recommender systems (content-based)
